paragraphs.text: [Meizhan](yancha:meizhan) (梅占) is a Fujian cultivar that came from Anxi, and this leaf was grown and made as [Wuyi rock tea](yancha:definition) in the Wuyi Mountains. It is less known than Rougui and Shui Xian, and it is not one of the four famous bushes of the range. As rock tea, the leaf is twisted into long strips and finished with a [charcoal roast](yancha:making) given in several rounds with rests between them, which dries the tea so it keeps.

The bushes of this area grow in [thin, stony ground](wuyi-mountains:nature) among cliffs and ravines, where rain is heavy, mist is common and the soil drains fast. The record names the range but not a zone, so it does not say how close to the [true rock core](wuyi-mountains:zones) this leaf grew.

Picked in 2024, the tea is two years old. Rock tea with a medium or full roast is the kind [kept for years](yancha:ageing), and the heavier the roast, the longer it is said to stay good, provided it is kept sealed, dry and cool.

brewing.text: Wuyi tea is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C, and about 5 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 120 ml gaiwan, a third to a half full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 5 to 20 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and good rock tea gives seven steeps or more. In a larger pot, use about 2 to 5 grams for 250 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: Roast and stone fruit, a mineral, rocky texture and a long, sweet, mouth-watering finish. Light roast is bright and floral, medium roast fruity and rounded, full roast charcoal, wood and roasted nuts. Da Hong Pao is often floral, Rougui spicy with cinnamon, young Shui Xian sweet and smooth, and old-bush Shui Xian woody and mossy.
